Prose is ordinary language — the natural way humans speak and write every day. When you write a letter, a text message, a school essay, a news article, or a novel, you are writing in prose. It is language that flows in sentences and paragraphs, following the natural rhythms of everyday speech.

The simplest way to put it: if it isn't poetry, it's almost certainly prose.
The One Contrast That Explains Everything

To truly understand prose, you need to compare it to its opposite: poetry.

Poetry is language that is carefully arranged into lines, and it usually follows a deliberate pattern — a rhythm, a beat, or a rhyme scheme. A poet counts syllables, chooses line breaks deliberately, and shapes the sound of the words as much as the meaning.

Prose does none of that. Prose just... flows. It doesn't follow a set beat or line pattern. A sentence in prose ends when the thought is complete — not when a rhythmic pattern demands it. There are no forced rhymes. No counting of syllables. The writer's only job is to communicate clearly and naturally.

Read this:

"It was a bright cold day in April, and the clocks were striking thirteen."

That is prose. It is one sentence. It ends because the idea is complete. Now read this:

"Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?
Thou art more lovely and more temperate."

That is poetry. Notice the deliberate line break, the rhythmic beat, the structured feel. The language is consciously shaped into a form.

Prose has no such rigid structure. It moves freely.
What Prose Looks Like in the Real World

Prose covers an enormous range of writing. Broadly, it splits into two categories:

1. Literary Prose
This is prose used as an art form — writing that aims to tell a story, explore characters, or express ideas in a beautiful and crafted way.

  • Novels — long fictional stories (Harry Potter, To Kill a Mockingbird)
  • Short stories — brief fictional narratives
  • Essays — a writer's thoughts and arguments on a topic, written in a personal or analytical voice
  • Memoirs and biographies — true accounts of people's lives

2. Everyday / Functional Prose
This is prose used purely to inform, instruct, or communicate — beauty is not the goal, clarity is.

  • News articles
  • Textbooks
  • Emails and letters
  • Legal documents
  • Instruction manuals
  • Encyclopaedia entries

Both are prose. The difference is the purpose and the level of craft, not the fundamental form.

No matter what kind of prose you are reading, it will always have these features:

Sentences. Prose is built from sentences — units of language with a subject and a verb that express a complete thought.

Paragraphs. Sentences are grouped into paragraphs. Each paragraph usually focuses on one idea, and then the next paragraph moves to the next idea.

Natural flow. Prose reads the way people naturally think and speak. There is no imposed beat forcing the writer to add or remove words to fit a rhythm.

No mandatory line breaks. Unlike poetry, a line of prose does not end until the sentence or paragraph is done. It fills the page from margin to margin.

Here is something important to understand: prose exists on a quality spectrum, and there are specific terms for the extremes.

Plain prose is simple, clear, and direct. It does its job without drawing attention to itself. Most functional writing — journalism, textbooks — aims for this.

Literary or elevated prose is crafted with care and beauty. The writer pays close attention to word choice, sentence rhythm, imagery, and tone. A gifted novelist doesn't just tell you what happened — they make you feel it. The sentences themselves become pleasurable to read.

Purple prose is what happens when a writer tries too hard. The language becomes over-the-top, dramatic, and flowery to the point of being distracting or even unintentionally funny. For example: "Her eyes were twin pools of shimmering azure moonlight, weeping crystalline rivers of sorrow down her porcelain cheeks." That is purple prose — too much, too ornate, too theatrical.
One Interesting Edge Case: Prose Poetry

Language doesn't always stay neatly in boxes. Prose poetry is a form that sits right on the border between prose and poetry. It is written in paragraphs (like prose), not in poetic lines, but it uses the rich, musical, image-heavy language of poetry. It has no strict meter, but it reads with unusual beauty and intensity. This shows that prose and poetry are really the two ends of a spectrum, not completely separate worlds.
The Word Used in a Sentence

You will often hear or read "prose" used in these ways:

  • "Hemingway was famous for his clean, spare prose." — referring to his writing style.
  • "The novel is written in beautiful prose." — meaning the language itself is elegantly written.
  • "Write your answer in prose, not bullet points." — meaning write in full sentences and paragraphs.
  • "She has a gift for prose." — meaning she is a naturally talented writer.

Prose is the ordinary, natural form of written or spoken language — structured in sentences and paragraphs, free from the fixed rhythms and line patterns of poetry — and it is the form used in everything from novels and essays to news articles and everyday conversation.
